passages.t: The king's letter, and the dream of the great tree
passages.happening:
This chapter is a letter from Nebuchadnezzar to ‘the people of every nation and language who dwell in all the earth’ (verse 1). He opens with praise: ‘His kingdom is an eternal kingdom; His dominion endures from generation to generation’ (verse 3).

Then he tells his story. He was at ease in his palace when a dream frightened him (verses 4-5). His wise men could not interpret it (verse 7). At last Daniel came in, and the king told him the dream (verses 8-9).

He saw a tree in the middle of the land. ‘The tree grew large and strong; its top reached the sky, and it was visible to the ends of the earth’ (verse 11). Its fruit fed everyone, beasts sheltered under it and birds nested in its branches (verse 12).

Then ‘a watcher, a holy one’ came down from heaven (verse 13) and called out: cut down the tree, strip it, scatter its fruit, but leave the stump with its roots in the ground, bound with iron and bronze (verses 14-15). Let him be drenched with dew and graze with the beasts. Let his mind be changed from a man's to a beast's until seven times pass (verses 15-16). The decree is given ‘so that the living will know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes, setting over it the lowliest of men’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Nebuchadnezzar has confessed Daniel's God twice already, as the revealer of mysteries and as the deliverer of the three men. Each time it stayed at the level of respect for a powerful god among others. In this chapter the lesson finally reaches the king himself, and it comes through humiliation.

The chapter is written as the king's own public letter, beginning and ending with praise. Most of it is in his own voice. In the Aramaic text and many printed Hebrew Bibles, verses 1 to 3 are numbered as the end of chapter 3, so the verse numbers differ by three from English Bibles.

A great tree at the center of the earth, sheltering beasts and birds, was a known picture of a great king or empire. Ezekiel pictures Assyria as a towering cedar cut down by God. The watchers are heavenly beings, holy ones who carry out God's decrees, and this is the only place in the Old Testament where the word appears. Their decree is pictured as coming from a heavenly council, as in 1 Kings 22 and Job 1.

The band of iron and bronze around the stump may suggest protection or restraint. Either way, the stump means the king's life and kingdom will be spared. The sentence of verse 17, that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind, is the key line of the chapter, and it will be repeated twice more.
passages.later: Ezekiel uses the same picture of a great tree for Assyria: ‘All the birds of the air nested in its branches’ (Ezekiel 31:6), until God cut it down because ‘it grew proud on account of its height’ (Ezekiel 31:10). Jesus' parable of the mustard seed uses the same picture for the kingdom of God, a tree where ‘the birds of the air come and nest in its branches’ (Matthew 13:32).
passages.asks: The king was at ease and flourishing when the warning came. Ask what your own success has made you stop noticing. And ask what it means that the dream was sent as a warning before it was a sentence.

passages.t: Daniel's interpretation, and his appeal to the king
passages.happening:
Daniel is perplexed and alarmed for a time. The king tells him not to be afraid. Daniel answers that he wishes the dream were about the king's enemies (verse 19).

Then he explains. The great tree is the king himself. ‘For you have become great and strong; your greatness has grown to reach the sky, and your dominion extends to the ends of the earth’ (verse 22). The decree of the Most High is against him (verse 24). ‘You will be driven away from mankind, and your dwelling will be with the beasts of the field’ (verse 25). He will eat grass like an ox until seven times pass, ‘until you acknowledge that the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes’ (verse 25). The stump means his kingdom will be restored ‘as soon as you acknowledge that Heaven rules’ (verse 26).

And Daniel pleads with him. ‘Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed. Perhaps there will be an extension of your prosperity’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Daniel does not enjoy delivering this word. He is troubled, and his first words are a wish that the dream were about someone else. He speaks to the king as a servant who cares what happens to him.

Notice what Daniel asks of the king. Not a religious ritual, but righteousness and mercy to the oppressed. The king's sin, in Daniel's eyes, was not only pride in his heart. It was the way his power had treated the poor. The first hearers, who had been among the oppressed of his empire, heard a Jewish exile tell the emperor to his face that he must show them mercy.

The word Perhaps matters. Daniel does not promise that repentance will cancel the sentence. He says it may lengthen the king's good years. The warning is given so that the king might turn.
passages.later: The prophet Micah says what the LORD requires: ‘to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God’ (Micah 6:8). And Proverbs gives the chapter's warning in one line: ‘Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall’ (Proverbs 16:18).
passages.asks: Daniel told a powerful man the truth, and he did it with care. Ask whether there is someone you need to warn, and whether you can do it as Daniel did, wishing them well. And ask who is oppressed by the power you hold, however small.

passages.t: The boast, and the sentence fulfilled
passages.happening:
‘All this happened to King Nebuchadnezzar’ (verse 28).

Twelve months later, walking on the roof of the royal palace, the king says, ‘Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built by the might of my power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?’ (verse 30).

While the words are still in his mouth, a voice comes from heaven. The kingdom has departed from him (verse 31). He will be driven from mankind and live with the beasts until seven times pass, until he acknowledges that the Most High rules (verse 32).

‘At that moment the sentence against Nebuchadnezzar was fulfilled’ (verse 33). He is driven away and eats grass like an ox, and his body is wet with dew until his hair grows like eagles' feathers and his nails like birds' claws.
passages.hearers:
Nebuchadnezzar really did rebuild Babylon on a grand scale. His own surviving inscriptions boast of its walls, palaces, temples and the Ishtar Gate, in language close to his boast in verse 30. The first hearers knew his reputation as the great builder.

A year passed between the warning and the fall. The sentence came while the boast was still in his mouth. In these verses the letter changes from the king's own voice to a narrator's, as if someone else must tell the part the king could not report.

The king who acted like a beast toward others is made to live like one until he looks up. The book's interest is not medical. Modern writers have compared his illness with known disorders in which a person believes himself an animal, but the chapter tells it as a sign of what pride does to a ruler.

Babylonian records that survive do not mention a time of madness in his reign. Records for his later years are sparse, and royal inscriptions rarely record a king's humiliation. A fragment among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Prayer of Nabonidus, tells of Babylon's last king, Nabonidus, struck with illness for seven years at Tema and healed when a Jewish diviner taught him to honor the Most High God.
passages.later: Isaiah mocks the king of Babylon who said, ‘I will make myself like the Most High’ (Isaiah 14:14). And in the next chapter Daniel reminds Belshazzar that his father ‘was deposed from his royal throne, and his glory was taken from him’ (Daniel 5:20).
passages.hard:
Is there evidence that Nebuchadnezzar went mad, and what does this story say about illness?

Surviving Babylonian sources do not record it. Scholars who read the chapter as history note that the records of his last three decades are fragmentary and that royal propaganda does not keep embarrassments, so the silence proves little. Many critical scholars point instead to the Prayer of Nabonidus and argue that an older story about Nabonidus has been retold of Nebuchadnezzar. Some read the chapter as a theological narrative whose truth does not depend on reconstructing the event. Readers across these views agree on what it teaches: the most powerful ruler of his age held his throne at God's pleasure.

This is the story of one king's pride and one judgment, told to show that the Most High rules. It is not a key for reading anyone else's illness. These notes do not read any person's mental illness, or any illness, as a punishment.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The king boasted of what he had ‘built by the might of my power’ (verse 30). Ask how often those words run through your own thoughts about what you have built. And ask what it would mean to give thanks for it instead.

passages.t: The king looks up, and praises the King of heaven
passages.happening:
‘But at the end of those days I, Nebuchadnezzar, looked up to heaven, and my sanity was restored to me’ (verse 34). The letter is back in his own voice. He praises the Most High: ‘For His dominion is an everlasting dominion, and His kingdom endures from generation to generation’ (verse 34).

All the peoples of the earth are as nothing before him, and he does as he pleases with heaven's army and earth's peoples. No one can hold back his hand or question him (verse 35).

The king's honor and splendor return, his advisers seek him out, and he is restored to his throne with even greater power (verse 36). He ends: ‘Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and exalt and glorify the King of heaven, for all His works are true and all His ways are just. And He is able to humble those who walk in pride’ (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
The turning point is small. The king looks up. For seven times he looked down at the grass like an animal. When he lifts his eyes to heaven, his mind comes back.

His praise at the end goes further than any of his earlier confessions. In chapter 2 Daniel's God was the revealer of mysteries. In chapter 3 he was the God who could deliver. Now he is the King of heaven, whose ways are just even when they humbled the king himself. The last word, that God is able to humble the proud, uses a verb, shephal, that will come back in the next chapter, when Belshazzar is condemned for not humbling his heart.

The first hearers, living under foreign kings, were given a remarkable picture: the greatest emperor of their memory, writing to the whole world that Israel's God had humbled him and that his ways are just. And they were given a warning for themselves too. Pride is the danger of everyone with power, not only of kings.
passages.later: Nebuchadnezzar's son Belshazzar knew this story, and Daniel tells him, ‘you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this’ (Daniel 5:22). Proverbs says the same of God: ‘He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble’ (Proverbs 3:34).
passages.asks: The king's mind came back when he looked up. Ask what you are looking at instead of heaven. And ask whether you are able to call God's ways just even in the things that humbled you.
